<dependency>

    <artifactId>spring-webflux</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

{"type":"output_text","text":{"value":"Let's clarify the concepts around `WebTestClient` in Spring Boot, as well as the confusion about a module called `spring-boot-starter-webtestclient`.

---

## 1. What is `WebTestClient`?

- `WebTestClient` is a **non-blocking, reactive client** for testing web applications.
- It is commonly used for testing Spring WebFlux applications, but it can also be used to test Spring MVC (servlet-based) applications.
- It works by issuing HTTP-like requests to your application, even without running it on a real server (if using mock setups).

---

## 2. What Dependency Should I Use?

There is **no official starter** called `spring-boot-starter-webtestclient`.  
Instead, you get `WebTestClient` support when you add one of the following dependencies:

### For Spring MVC (Servlet)
- Add the regular `spring-boot-starter-test`, which already includes all you need (such as `spring-test` and more):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

### For Spring WebFlux (Reactive)
- The same `spring-boot-starter-test` covers both MVC and WebFlux testing, including `WebTestClient`, plus `spring-boot-starter-webflux` **if your app is reactive**:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

> **In short:**  
> There is no such thing as `spring-boot-starter-webtestclient`.  
> Use `spring-boot-starter-test` instead, which provides `WebTestClient` support for your tests.

---

## 3. Basic Usage Example

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
public class MyControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @Test
    public void testGetEndpoint() {
        webTestClient.get()
            .uri("/my-endpoint")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}
```

---

## **Summary Table**

| Feature | Dependency Required                        |
|---------|-------------------------------------------|
| WebTestClient (for web tests) | `spring-boot-starter-test` (for both MVC and WebFlux) |
| WebFlux App itself           | `spring-boot-starter-webflux`     |

---

**References:**  
- [Spring WebTestClient Documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/testing/webtestclient.html)
- [Spring Boot Test Starters](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/html/features.html#features.testing)","annotations":null},"bing_searches":null,"annotations":null}

{"type":"output_text","text":{"value":"If you want to use `WebTestClient` in a Spring Boot project with Maven, you need to include the correct dependencies. `WebTestClient` is part of Spring’s web testing framework and is mostly used for testing reactive web applications, but it can also test Servlet-based apps.

## Maven Dependency for WebTestClient

For **Spring Boot 2.x/3.x**, include:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

- `spring-boot-starter-webflux` brings in the `WebTestClient` class.
- `spring-boot-starter-test` gives you additional testing support.

> **Note:**  
> Even if your app isn’t reactive, using WebTestClient for tests is perfectly fine; just don’t include WebFlux as a non-test dependency unless your app is reactive!

## Example Usage

```java
import org.springframework.test.web.reactive.server.WebTestClient;

@WebFluxTest
public class MyControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @Test
    public void testMyEndpoint() {
        webTestClient.get().uri("/my-endpoint")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}
```

## Summary Table

| Dependency                         | When Required     |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------|
| spring-boot-starter-test            | Always            |
| spring-boot-starter-webflux (test)  | For WebTestClient |

If you want the latest safe versions, you can always check [Maven Central](https://search.maven.org/) or the [Spring Boot documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/html/dependency-versions.html).

Let me know if you want the most up-to-date version numbers or a working example!","annotations":null},"bing_searches":null,"annotations":null}

{"type":"output_text","text":{"value":"With **Spring Boot 3.5**, you use `WebTestClient` for testing WebFlux applications and, increasingly, for testing regular (Servlet-based) MVC apps thanks to the common test improvements. Here’s what you need to know about using `spring-boot-webtestclient` in Spring Boot 3.5:

---

## 1. **Dependency**

If you're using Maven, add this to your `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

Or, if you want ONLY the testing utilities:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

This starter now **includes `WebTestClient`** for both MVC and WebFlux contexts.

---

## 2. **Basic Usage Example**

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
public class MyWebTests {

    @Autowired
    private WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @Test
    void testGetEndpoint() {
        webTestClient.get()
                .uri("/api/something")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk()
                .expectBody()
                .jsonPath("$.name").isEqualTo("MyValue");
    }
}
```

---

## 3. **What’s New in Spring Boot 3.5?**

- **Native support across WebFlux and MVC** – `WebTestClient` can be used for both stack types, not just WebFlux APIs.
- **Auto-configuration** makes setup easier with `@AutoConfigureWebTestClient`.
- Works seamlessly with JUnit 5 for modern testing.

---

## 4. **No Separate “spring-boot-webtestclient” Module**

There is **no separate artifact** called `spring-boot-webtestclient`; just use `spring-boot-starter-test`, which already includes everything.

---

## 5. **Docs Reference**

For more details:
- [Spring Boot 3.5 Release Notes](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/releases)
- [WebTestClient in Official Docs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/html/testing.html#testing.webtestclient)

---

**Summary:**  
Use `spring-boot-starter-test` and `@AutoConfigureWebTestClient` in your test classes. `WebTestClient` works out of the box in Spring Boot 3.5 for both MVC and WebFlux controllers.

{"type":"output_text","text":{"value":"When **migrating from an earlier version of Spring Boot to 4.0**, there are several important updates to be aware of, especially regarding testing dependencies and API changes.

### 1. `spring-boot-starter-test` in Spring Boot 4.0

- `spring-boot-starter-test` is still the main starter for testing in Spring Boot 4.0.
- It brings in the key testing dependencies (JUnit Jupiter, Mockito, AssertJ, etc).
- In Spring Boot 4.0, the starter now includes more recent dependency versions (JUnit 5.10, Mockito 5.x, etc).

### 2. `spring-boot-webtestclient`

- `WebTestClient` is a non-blocking, reactive web test client introduced in Spring 5, used for testing WebFlux and, to some extent, servlet apps.
- There is **no separate starter** called `spring-boot-webtestclient`.
- Instead, `WebTestClient` is included transitively via the `spring-boot-starter-test` if you have either WebFlux or Web MVC on your classpath.

### 3. Changes in Spring Boot 4.0

#### - JUnit 4 Support Removed
- JUnit 4 support is dropped. All tests should use JUnit 5 (JUnit Jupiter).
- If you have tests annotated with JUnit 4 (`@RunWith`, etc.), migrate them to JUnit 5 (`@ExtendWith`, etc).

#### - Mockito & Other Testing Libraries
- Versions of Mockito, AssertJ, and others have been updated to recent major versions to ensure compatibility with Java 17+.
- Make sure your custom configurations or extensions still work with the new versions.

#### - Test Configuration Changes
- Some annotations and test configurations have been deprecated or replaced. Review your use of annotations such as `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, and similar.

#### - API or Behavioral Changes
- Review the [Spring Boot 4.0 migration guide](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-4.0-Migration-Guide) for details on deprecated/removed APIs.
- Some third-party or internal test utility methods may be incompatible due to library upgrades.

### 4. How to Migrate Your Test Code

- **Dependencies:**  
  In your `pom.xml` or `build.gradle`, make sure you only use:
  ```xml
  <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
      <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  ```
  Remove any explicit dependency on `spring-boot-webtestclient` (it does not exist as a separate artifact).

- **Using `WebTestClient`:**
  With Spring Boot 4, `WebTestClient` usage remains the same as previous Spring 2.x & 3.x versions. Just autowire or instantiate it in your tests.

- **JUnit 4 -> JUnit 5 Migration Example:**
  **Old:**
  ```java
  @RunWith(SpringRunner.class)
  @SpringBootTest
  public class MyTest { ... }
  ```
  **New:**
  ```java
  @SpringBootTest
  class MyTest { ... }
  // Use @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, etc.
  ```

- **Migrate any old test code** that used now-removed or deprecated features.

### 5. References & Resources

- [Spring Boot 4.0 Migration Guide](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-4.0-Migration-Guide)
- [Spring Boot 4.0 Release Notes](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/releases/tag/v4.0.0)

---

**In summary:**  
- Use only `spring-boot-starter-test` for test dependencies.
- `WebTestClient` is provided by the core Spring testing stack.
- Remove any `spring-boot-webtestclient` dependency (it does not exist).
- Migrate all tests to JUnit Jupiter (JUnit 5).
- Double-check for deprecated APIs and other potential breaking changes.

Let me know if you have questions about a specific test configuration or piece of code!","annotations":null},"bing_searches":null,"annotations":null}

    "value": "When **migrating from an earlier version of Spring Boot to 4.0**, there are several important updates to be aware of, especially regarding testing dependencies and API changes.

### 1. `spring-boot-starter-test` in Spring Boot 4.0

- `spring-boot-starter-test` is still the main starter for testing in Spring Boot 4.0.
- It brings in the key testing dependencies (JUnit Jupiter, Mockito, AssertJ, etc).
- In Spring Boot 4.0, the starter now includes more recent dependency versions (JUnit 5.10, Mockito 5.x, etc).

### 2. `spring-boot-webtestclient`

- `WebTestClient` is a non-blocking, reactive web test client introduced in Spring 5, used for testing WebFlux and, to some extent, servlet apps.
- There is **no separate starter** called `spring-boot-webtestclient`.
- Instead, `WebTestClient` is included transitively via the `spring-boot-starter-test` if you have either WebFlux or Web MVC on your classpath.

### 3. Changes in Spring Boot 4.0

#### - JUnit 4 Support Removed
- JUnit 4 support is dropped. All tests should use JUnit 5 (JUnit Jupiter).
- If you have tests annotated with JUnit 4 (`@RunWith`, etc.), migrate them to JUnit 5 (`@ExtendWith`, etc).

#### - Mockito & Other Testing Libraries
- Versions of Mockito, AssertJ, and others have been updated to recent major versions to ensure compatibility with Java 17+.
- Make sure your custom configurations or extensions still work with the new versions.

#### - Test Configuration Changes
- Some annotations and test configurations have been deprecated or replaced. Review your use of annotations such as `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, and similar.

#### - API or Behavioral Changes
- Review the [Spring Boot 4.0 migration guide](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-4.0-Migration-Guide) for details on deprecated/removed APIs.
- Some third-party or internal test utility methods may be incompatible due to library upgrades.

### 4. How to Migrate Your Test Code

- **Dependencies:**  
  In your `pom.xml` or `build.gradle`, make sure you only use:
  ```xml
  <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
      <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  ```
  Remove any explicit dependency on `spring-boot-webtestclient` (it does not exist as a separate artifact).

- **Using `WebTestClient`:**
  With Spring Boot 4, `WebTestClient` usage remains the same as previous Spring 2.x & 3.x versions. Just autowire or instantiate it in your tests.

- **JUnit 4 -> JUnit 5 Migration Example:**
  **Old:**
  ```java
  @RunWith(SpringRunner.class)
  @SpringBootTest
  public class MyTest { ... }
  ```
  **New:**
  ```java
  @SpringBootTest
  class MyTest { ... }
  // Use @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, etc.
  ```

- **Migrate any old test code** that used now-removed or deprecated features.

### 5. References & Resources

- [Spring Boot 4.0 Migration Guide](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-4.0-Migration-Guide)
- [Spring Boot 4.0 Release Notes](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/releases/tag/v4.0.0)

- Use only `spring-boot-starter-test` for test dependencies.
- `WebTestClient` is provided by the core Spring testing stack.
- Remove any `spring-boot-webtestclient` dependency (it does not exist).
- Migrate all tests to JUnit Jupiter (JUnit 5).
- Double-check for deprecated APIs and other potential breaking changes.
